nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
The Marquee still smells of velvet, dust, and Noah’s terrible coffee. Five days until reopening. Five days to make something beautiful—and decide how much of my own mess to admit.

Noah is waiting beside the ladder I used at nineteen. Eli lowers his camera as I enter.

nodes.speaker: ELI
nodes.text:
“Before I point this at you: may I film the first poster going up? You can say no.”

Noah steadies the ladder. “She usually makes the posters look good by insulting my lettering.”

“Your lettering has grown as a person,” I tell him. “Unfortunately, not as lettering.”

choices.text: Let Eli film the poster, but keep me out of the shot.
Ask Eli to put the camera away for now.

nodes.speaker: ELI
nodes.text:
“Poster only. Got it.” Eli turns the monitor so I can check the frame. My face is nowhere in it.

I hand Noah the tape. He has already torn off three pieces and stuck them to his sleeve. Some kinds of intimacy are embarrassingly practical.

nodes.speaker: NOAH
nodes.text:
Eli switches the camera off and puts it in its bag. “Then I can be useful without evidence.”

Noah hands him the tape. “A radical new direction for documentary.”

For a moment, we are just three people trying to hang a poster straight.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
An orange tag hangs from the old projector case. MONDAY COLLECTION. I glance at Noah. He folds the tag beneath the handle a little too quickly.

My phone lights up: CHICAGO INTERVIEW — MONDAY. I turn it face down. Apparently, I am not the only person with a Monday problem.

choices.text: Ask Noah what is being collected on Monday.
Keep the evening gentle. Ask about the tag later.

nodes.speaker: NOAH
nodes.text:
“The projector. Unless I find four thousand dollars by Sunday.” Noah looks at the poster: SAVE THE ANALOG HEART.

“The deposit paid the staff. I should have told you before you designed that.”

Eli leaves his camera in its bag. Nobody reaches for an easy joke.

nodes.speaker: NOAH
nodes.text:
“That corner needs another inch,” Noah says. We adjust the poster together. The orange tag stays tucked out of sight.

Eli steps back. “People are going to want to know what they’re saving.”

He means the campaign. Or perhaps all three of us do.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
The poster cannot promise something we may sell. That part is clear. What is less clear is how I can ask for honesty while calling my own layoff a sabbatical.

Noah waits for my answer. Eli waits without recording it.

choices.text: Tell them about the layoff and Chicago. Then rewrite the promise together.
Ask for the full budget before offering help. Keep my own news private tonight.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
The poster is finally straight. Noah asks how long my “sabbatical” lasts. Eli asks what I want to make next.

Two reasonable questions. One carefully maintained fiction.

I could tell them why I really came home—or give myself one more evening.

choices.text: Tell them I lost my job and have an interview in Chicago.
Say I’m still figuring it out, and take a little space tonight.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
“I was laid off. And I have an interview in Chicago on Monday.”

Noah exhales. “Then I don’t get to build a rescue plan around you staying.”

Eli pulls a blank sheet from my portfolio. “What can this poster honestly promise?”

We settle on ONE MORE FIRST NIGHT. A beginning, not a guarantee. When Noah passes me the pen, his hand rests beside mine. This time, neither of us pretends not to notice.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
I tell them about the layoff. Then Chicago. Saying it aloud makes it sound less like a verdict.

“You don’t have to earn your place here by saving the building,” Noah says. Eli asks whether I want company while I work on my portfolio. He waits for an answer.

I haven’t decided. That feels different from hiding.

On my way out, I notice the orange tag again. Tomorrow, I will ask.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
“Show me the numbers tomorrow. I can help with the campaign, but I can’t promise to fix this.”

Noah nods. “Fair.” He writes BUDGET — 9 AM on the back of a ticket.

Eli opens the door for me, camera still packed away. “Coffee before the meeting?”

“Actual coffee?”

“An ambitious proposal. I know.”

I leave with an invitation, a boundary, and my own news still unsaid.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
“I’m still figuring it out. Tonight, I think I need a walk.”

Noah offers my coat. Eli asks if I want company. I shake my head, and he lets the question end there.

Outside, the first bulbs of the marquee blink awake. I take a photograph—not for the campaign, just for me.

Tomorrow holds a poster, an orange tag, and two people I want to understand. Tonight can belong to me.

nodes.speaker: NOAH
nodes.text:
By nine the next morning, Noah has spread the budget across the ticket counter. Beside it sits our revised poster: ONE MORE FIRST NIGHT.

“I called the buyer. Collection is Monday afternoon. We have until Sunday night to return the deposit.”

He slides me a coffee. “And your interview comes first. I wrote that down too.”

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
At nine, I point to the orange tag before anyone can offer me coffee. Noah takes a breath. The old projector is sold unless he can return a four-thousand-dollar deposit by Sunday. The money paid the staff.

“You knew when we hung the poster?”

“Yes. I wanted one evening when you were glad to be back.”

“I was. You could have trusted that.” We take down the promise to save the projector and start again.

nodes.speaker: ELI
nodes.text:
Eli arrives with two coffees and a receipt, as though proving that neither came from Noah’s machine.

“No strings,” he says. “Not even a loyalty card.”

Inside, Noah has the budget ready. The missing four thousand dollars is real; so is the list of staff he paid with the deposit. I draw a line around what I can offer: one campaign, no personal loan. He leaves the line where I put it.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
My walk gave me no miraculous answers, only enough sleep to ask a clear question. At nine, I ask Noah about the orange tag.

He explains the projector sale and the wages the deposit covered. I am angry that he hid it, relieved the staff were paid, and annoyed that both things can be true.

“We cannot sell people a rescue we cannot promise,” I say. Together we take down yesterday’s poster.

nodes.speaker: ELI
nodes.text:
Eli puts his phone beside the revised poster. A documentary producer has offered him a paid meeting if he can send a strong sample by tonight.

“She suggested a homecoming love story,” he says. “I said you weren’t characters I could cast without asking.”

Noah studies him. “But you still want the meeting.”

“Yes. I want work. I also want to be able to look you both in the eye afterward.”

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
We have one evening to bring people through the doors. Enough ticket pledges could return the deposit, but nobody can promise it. Eli can film the building without turning our private lives into the hook.

What kind of invitation do I want to put my name on?

choices.text: Make a public appeal: show the real deadline and where the money goes.
Invite the neighborhood to a small preview. Keep it personal and off camera.

nodes.speaker: ELI
nodes.text:
We record the empty auditorium, the repair receipts, and Noah explaining the deadline. Eli gives us the cut before he posts it. Nothing private has slipped into the frame.

The first pledges arrive with practical questions. Who holds the money? What happens if we miss the target? We put the answers beside the booking button.

It is less romantic than a rescue montage. It is also the first version I believe.

nodes.speaker: NOAH
nodes.text:
Noah calls the baker next door. I write invitations on the backs of unused tickets. Eli puts his camera away and carries chairs.

Twelve people promise to come. Then eighteen. Someone offers a tray of food, which does not pay for a projector but does make an evening feel possible.

“We may still lose it,” Noah says.

“Then we will have told people the truth before they arrived.”

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
The invitations are out. For the first time all day, there is an hour nobody has filled for me. Noah is testing the booth. Eli is sorting through his sample footage. My portfolio waits in my bag.

Who gets that hour?

choices.text: Join Noah in the booth and talk about what changed between us.
Help Eli choose his sample, and ask what he wants beyond the film.
Work on my portfolio. Let tonight include my own future.

nodes.speaker: NOAH
nodes.text:
Noah shows me a strip of film held against the booth light. At nineteen, I thought loving this place meant never leaving it.

“I used to make staying sound like proof,” he says. “That was unfair to you.”

I tell him about Monday: Chicago, an interview, no promise of a job. This time I leave nothing hidden.

“I would like dinner with you,” he says. “Somewhere with no fundraising jar.” I say I would like that too. It is a date, not an agreement to stay.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
The public appeal has brought in twenty-three hundred dollars in pledges. Enough to make a difference. Not enough to buy certainty.

The first guests are waiting under the marquee. Noah asks whether I want to speak. Eli leaves the camera lowered.

What promise am I willing to make in front of this room?

choices.text: Promise one more honest evening together, with a clear limit on my help.
Tell them I am leaving for my interview, and hand the next step to the community.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
“I can help through Sunday,” I tell them. “I can promise good work. I cannot promise a miracle.”

Noah repeats the deadline without softening it. Tomorrow I will help, and Monday I will still take my interview.

The appeal continues after the screening. The projector’s future remains open, but the accounts and deadline are there for everyone to see.

After the applause, Noah slips a blank ticket into my hand. On the back: DINNER. NO FUNDRAISING.

“After Chicago?” he asks.

“After the interview. We can work out the geography.” His hand finds mine without asking it to hold the building up.

End of prototype chapter — The Last First Night. The next chapter will be shaped by player feedback.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
“I have an interview in Chicago on Monday,” I say. “This place matters to me. So does finding out what comes next.”

I hand the campaign notes to the volunteer at the ticket desk. Leaving a task in other hands feels strange, then lighter.

The appeal continues after the screening. The projector’s future remains open, but the accounts and deadline are there for everyone to see.

nodes.speaker: ELI
nodes.text:
Eli’s strongest shot is of Noah teaching a teenager to thread the projector. Nobody is confessing anything. Everybody is paying attention.

“That one,” I say.

“The producer may think it is too quiet.” He sends it anyway.

I tell him about Chicago and ask where he expects to be next month. “I don’t know. But I’d like to take you out before we both mistake uncertainty for a reason not to ask.”

I say yes to dinner. Only dinner. He smiles as though that is plenty.

nodes.speaker: MAYA
nodes.text:
I spread my portfolio across the back row. For forty minutes I choose work I am proud of, instead of work that proves I am useful to someone else.

When the others return, I tell them plainly: I lost my job. I have an interview in Chicago on Monday. I intend to go.

Noah asks if I want another pair of eyes on the layout. Eli asks before moving the lamp. Neither tries to turn the news into a vote.

For once, being cared for does not interrupt what I came to do.
